items.title: Jalen Green could be the key to a more dynamic Suns offense
items.content:
PHOENIX, ARIZONA - APRIL 17: Jalen Green #4 of the Phoenix Suns reacts after a three-point shot against the Golden State Warriors during the second half of an NBA play-in tournament game at Mortgage Matchup Center on April 17, 2026 in Phoenix, Arizona. The Suns defeated the Warriors 111-96. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images	How will the Suns’ offense function next season? Will it become predictable again, like it did last year? The Suns weren’t exactly running a complex offense down the stretch, and far too many possessions ended with a three-point attempt. 

From February 1 on, Phoenix went 15–18. And during that span, 46.9% of its shots came from beyond the arc. That ranked sixth in the league. They were also third in the NBA in the percentage of their total points that came from three-point range at 41.5%. That’s something the Suns have to change next season because, quite simply, it didn’t work. They need more ways to generate offense. Having players who can get downhill, attack the rim, and create pressure inside is something this team desperately needs.

Suns’ CEO Josh Bartelstein was on with Burns and Gambo earlier this week, and he said that “The league right now has evolved so much. Where the league was three or four years ago, where shooting was in high demand…of course you wanna have shooters…if you watch what’s happening now, it’s guys who can get downhill. Get two feet in the paint. It’s guys who can guard multiple positions. It’s athletic specimens who can meet you at the rim and block your shot. You got to be able to attack and play off closeouts and spray the ball around.”

Why were the Phoenix Suns willing to pay the price to acquire Miles Bridges?

CEO of the Suns and Mercury Josh Bartelstein explained their thought process earlier today.

Full interview: https://t.co/9uKCqzh2hmpic.twitter.com/rBOnxf1bV3

— The Burns & Gambo Show (@BurnsAndGambo) August 5, 2026The conversation centered on the acquisition of Miles Bridges and how he could ultimately affect the offense. That naturally leads to another interesting question: Who will be the second-leading scorer on this team next season, assuming Devin Booker remains the top dog? Because if he isn’t, the Suns are going to have a multitude of other problems.

The majority of the community believes Jalen Green will fill that role. In our most recent Suns Reacts survey, 61% of voters picked Green to finish second on the team in scoring. Miles Bridges came in second at 22%.

I agree with the consensus that Jalen Green will be the second leading scorer for Phoenix next season. His talent, combined with his athleticism, should create plenty of opportunities for him to fill that role. items.title: On this day in Bucks history: Milwaukee signs Bobby Simmons
items.content:
ST. FRANCIS, WI - AUGUST 8: Larry Harris, Milwaukee Bucks General Manager (L) introduces Bobby Simmons (R) to the media during a press conference at the Milwaukee Bucks Training Center on August 8, 2005 in St. Francis, Wisconsin. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory copyright notice: Copyright NBAE 2005. (Photo by Gary Dineen/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images	I can remember it vividly. Year 11 (junior year to most of you). My best friend’s voice riding the wind across the yard.

“Did you see it?”

I looked up, mouth ajar, eyes staring as if I was mid matrices exam. Then the follow-up.

“The Bucks have signed Bobby Simmons!”

Dilation. Pupils, mouth. Everything.

It was true. A quick—okay, slow (we’re talking ADSL speeds)—Google search (or was it Ask Jeeves?) confirmed the news. The NBA’s reigning Most Improved Player (MIP), coming off a season in which he averaged 16.4 PPG, 5.9 RPG, 2.7 APG, and 1.4 SPG on .466/.435/.846 shooting, was joining the Bucks on a 5-year $47m contract.

And they were movin’ on up. 

The promiseMy excitement was palpable, even as a closet fan. Coming off a 25th-placed 30-52 season the year prior, Simmons’ arrival signalled change and upward trajectory in Milwaukee. But he wasn’t alone. T.J. Ford—yes, that new assistant coach—was back after missing his entire sophomore season due to a severe spinal injury, Michael Redd had just re-signed on a six-year deal (remember those?), and Andrew Bogut had arrived in town after being selected with the number one overall pick in the NBA Draft. Youth and promise. Sounds familiar, right? Oh, and they had a new coach too, moving off one Terry (Porter) for another (Stotts). 

But the roster revitalisation wasn’t done. Not yet. Two months later, Milwaukee would trade for All-Star centre Jamaal Magloire in a deal that sent out Desmond Mason and a 2006 first-round pick (that would become Cedric Simmons). And just like that, the starters were set: two seven-footers up front, a big-bodied forward on the wing, a sweet-shooting two, and an exciting, young point. Read that sentence again and you could easily confuse it for this year’s squad.

So, with a revamped starting five that also strengthened the bench—2004-05 starters Joe Smith, Mo Williams, and Dan Gadzuric became reserves—the Bucks looked primed for a playoff push. 

Bright beginningsThe season started with a bang—a 117-108 overtime win against the Philadelphia 76ers—and Simmons looked every bit the key free agent signing Bucks fans had hoped for, dropping 22 points to go along with a career-high-tying 12 rebounds. Up next, New Jersey. Kidd, Vince, RJ. SEGABABA. items.title: Pistons Notes: Duren, Roster Crunch, Ball-Handling, East
items.content:
Although the Pistons remain determined to re-sign restricted free agent Jalen Duren, they have “drawn a line in the sand” in terms of how much money they’re willing to offer the All-NBA big man, writes Omari Sankofa II of The Detroit Free Press (subscriber link).

Sankofa speculates that the contract standoff could last until October 1, which is Duren’s deadline to potentially accept a one-year, $9.6MM qualifying offer to become an unrestricted free agent next year. The two sides could agree to push back that deadline, but Sankofa doesn’t expect that to happen, since neither party would benefit from letting the situation linger into the regular season.

Appearing on NBA Today earlier this week (YouTube link), University of Memphis head coach Penny Hardaway said it was “very important” to Duren to re-sign with the Pistons. The former NBA star was Duren’s coach during the 22-year-old’s lone college season with the Tigers.

“Jalen is a guy that … he wants to finish where he started,” Hardaway said. “He’s very loyal. And he’s gonna play his heart out for Detroit. He wants to win a championship there. … They’ve only scratched the surface, and with him being an All-Star for the first time (last year), his heart and soul is in Detroit. So hopefully that all works itself out.”

Here’s more on the Pistons:

Within that same subscriber-only story, Sankofa takes a look at Detroit’s roster crunch, pointing out that the team will have 16 players on standard deals if Duren returns as expected. Sankofa believes the final roster spot could come down to Taurean Prince or Gary Harris, two veterans who were acquired from Milwaukee this offseason in a cost-cutting move. When we previewed possible NBA roster crunches last month, we speculated that Harris might be the odd man out, but noted that there’s still time for additional moves to be made before late October, when the regular season begins.
The Pistons addressed one of their main offseason needs by bolstering their outside shooting with the acquisitions of Isaiah Joe and John Collins, but did they add enough ball-handling to relieve play-making pressure off Cade Cunningham? Coty M. Davis of The Detroit News (subscription required) thinks the answer to that question is no, since it may take No. 17 overall pick Ebuka Okorie some time to adjust to the NBA based on his Summer League play. Still, the team’s relative lack of activity on that front is a sign that it believes in Daniss Jenkins as a secondary ball-handler, Davis writes, with Ausar Thompson likely to handle tertiary play-making duties.
